text:
Now I know that gold is a classic rare metal that people should have some exposure to in their accounts anyway, but I think there is potential for a longer run over the coming years, so I am going to make my bull case and bear case. I already have a small position, but I am also planning on purchasing more at the current prices. My ETF of choice is GLD since it tracks the spot price directly and also has an annual expense ratio of 0.4%. If anyone prefers a different method, feel free to say as much in the comments. I have considered buying physical as well.

My Bull Case for buying @ ~$366

GLD sits about 28% below its 52-week high of $509.70. I realize the run up was a good selling opportunity, but gold is still hovering near $4,000 after a sharp pullback. I feel like investors typically fall into two camps after a big correction: this is either a good opportunity to buy in, or the rally is over. So why'd it drop so much? A combo of interest rate expectations, Treasury yield increases, and the dollar momentarily strengthening. I’ll touch on this more in the bear case.

Over the last 25 years, gold has outperformed the S&P by about double (938% vs 461%). I know 25 years is pretty arbitrary as far as time horizons go, but I am planning on holding for a long time.

The US federal debt keeps climbing and climbing. In fiscal year 2026 we hit a record $1.05 trillion in net interest payments. I repeat - over $1T on interest alone! How is the US government planning on reining this in? In my opinion, the likeliest path forward is policies that tolerate inflation and erode the true value of the debt. I foresee a lot of money printing in the near future. In this case, people holding cash lose out.

Have the structural reasons for buying gold changed in the last few years? Has the US eliminated its fiscal deficit? Has the debt begun shrinking? Has federal interest expense returned to historical norms? Have the central banks stopped diversifying reserves? Has the global monetary system suddenly become more disciplined? I am inclined to say no to all of these questions. The short-term circumstances for gold provide some pretty strong headwinds (see the bear case), but I think the long-term forces still apply.

Gold still matters from a de-dollarization perspective. No fiat currency has ever survived in the history of mankind, and the US dollar can go the same way. Gold can’t be printed like fiat, and there is continued instability in the Middle East. That cuts both ways, though - the conflict supports gold as a safe haven, but it has also strengthened the dollar and kept energy prices elevated (again see bear case).

As far as following the “smart” money goes, central banks bought over 1,000 metric tons a year from 2022 through 2024, and still added 863 tons in 2025.

A minor, but legitimate, player is the AI build out. Gold in electronics accounts for ~7% of annual gold demand, compared to jewelry, central bank buying, and investment demand. Figured I would include it since this is a global movement.

My Bear Case for avoiding @ ~$366

Gold pays no yield, and higher interest rates or other strong performing assets apply pressure or are at least tempting/more exciting.

A stronger dollar can pressure it, as we’ve seen recently, even if its momentary.

Reuters reported on Oct 12 that the dollar was near its strongest level in a year and a half, helped by safe-haven demand amid the war in Iran. Higher energy prices are likely to keep inflation elevated, and the SPR is at historic lows. Pressure on other routes to get oil out of the Middle East is exacerbating this.

All of this points to Warsh keeping interest rates high or pushing them higher. Keep in mind that we are expecting another Fed rate decision on Oct 28, and a hike is definitely on the table.

The 30 year Treasury bonds are at ~5.3%.

Some critics think the growth of the US economy could outpace the debt (I don’t personally agree with this).

Possible PT?

Just using this part to say that historical performance is not a guarantee of future price action. Gold can always stop climbing for a number of reasons, and just because gold’s historical rebounds from large corrections have seen it climb higher doesn’t mean that will happen again. Not financial advice, lol.

Quick math on a possible 5-year price target using gold’s 25-year return (938%):

The multiple of a 938% return = 938/100 + 1 = 10.38x

Annualized return over 25 years = 10.38^(1/25) - 1 = 1.098 - 1 = 0.098, or 9.8% a year

Applying that rate for 5 years = 1.098^5 = ~1.6x

Apply that multiple to the current price: $366 * 1.6 = ~$586. Shave off about 2% for fees and call it ~$575.

That’s about $65 above the 52-week high of $509.70, or roughly 57% above today’s price. That doesn't seem like much in this crazy bull market, but since it is the world reserve asset, I think it is a good play in this environment. I plan to DCA my position over the next few months. Can it can go lower? Yup, I just know I am not buying at the top! Thoughts?

Xiaomi shipped 30.7 million smartphones in the third quarter, down 29.2% from a year earlier, according to IDC's preliminary vendor table. Samsung and Apple between them held 45.0% of the quarter's shipments, up from 36.9% a year earlier. Both OPPO and vivo fell by larger percentages than Xiaomi.

The full market came in at 255.3 million units, and IDC put the year-over-year decline at 22.0%, calling it the largest of any quarter in its tracking. Counterpoint Research, in preliminary figures released October 12, had the decline at 20%. IDC published its figures on October 14; both firms count vendor shipments, not sales to consumers, and both sets of numbers are subject to revision. IDC expects overall smartphone growth to be constrained through 2027, with any recovery pushed to 2028 at the earliest.

I put those numbers next to Xiaomi's second quarter results from August 18, where phones were about 39% of revenue. Shipments fell to 31.2 million from 42.4 million a year earlier. Xiaomi said its second quarter shipment drop was mainly from optimizing its product portfolio and cutting mid-range and low-end volumes, and also from weakening global demand as key component costs kept rising. The average smartphone selling price rose to a record 1,351 yuan.

That reads as a company trading units for a higher average price. But the same second quarter report put phone gross margin at 8.5%, down from 11.5% a year earlier, so a record average price has not translated into a stronger margin. Memory costs are still climbing, according to IDC's Nabila Popal, though the quarter-over-quarter increase slowed to low double digits in the third quarter. I have not seen Xiaomi's third quarter phone margin yet, so whether that trade works is still open.

With component costs still climbing, have you or the people around you started waiting longer between phone upgrades?

Meta's Free Cash Flow yield is 1.7%, but this is no longer a very useful metric to use because of Meta's high reinvestment rate into future growth projects. A better metric would be EV/OCF, which sits at ~12.5. But adjusting for SBC expense (an exorbitant 7.2 billion in the last quarter alone), we reach an EV/(adjusted) OCF of 16.1.

Many people claim the business is grossly undervalued, including now, but the clear time to buy was in 2022. At this time it reached an EV/OCF of 4.3 and a SBC-adjusted value of 6.3.

As per value investing principles, the right time to buy a stock is usually when the business is out of favor. In 2022, it was definitely out of favor. Apple's privacy changes were disrupting the ads business, capex was flooding into metaverse development (low interest and uncertain ROI), and margins contracted down to 20%.

There was certainly reason to be scared out of holding the stock, but the legend goes the best time to buy a stock is when is feels the most uncomfortable. In Meta's case, if you like founder-led companies with skin in the game, Meta in 2022 gave you that cushion because we all knew Zuck was not going to stop innovating. His track record more or less proves that. Similar to the 2008 GFC, sometimes you have to invest in the unknown and understand there is a small chance things won't work out, but that the risk reward is very favorable to make you $ if you are right.

If you invested at $155 in 2022, despite the stock contracting another 42% later into the year, you would have still made ~310% up to today, which is a 43% CAGR.

Today, Meta is not ridiculously undervalued (at least using historical context) and more than likely, you will earn a return in line with free cash flow per share growth over time, not including any multiple expansion. "Undervalued" is being thrown around quite a bit but it might be valuable to take current prices into perspective.

text:
Form 4s actually matter (with two live examples)
Company Analysis
Every quarter someone posts "insiders dumped $XXB!!" and the top reply is "nothing burger, it's stock comp." Both are partly right. Here's the 60-second filter I use on a Form 4 before I take it seriously.

1. Check the transaction code

S = open-market sale

P = open-market purchase

F = shares withheld to pay tax on vesting

M = option exercise

F and M are almost always noise. Most of the scary headline totals are S trades plus a pile of these.

2. Check the 10b5-1 box Since April 2023, Form 4 has a checkbox showing whether a trade was made under a pre-arranged trading plan. Planned sales were scheduled months earlier and carry little information.

3. Look for cluster buys after a drawdown Several insiders buying with their own cash after a big drop is the classic signal. Live example from last week, straight from EDGAR:

Rapport Therapeutics (RAPP), 21–23 Oct 2026:

6 insiders bought: the CFO plus five directors

7 open-market purchases, about $1.66M total

Prices between $26.10 and $27.36

The largest was a director buying 35,714 shares (~$974K)

The CEO's only Form 4 that week was a small sale (2,210 shares, ~$64K), so "CEO buying" claims floating around are wrong

That's the pattern people look for: several board members writing checks at once after the stock fell hard. It still isn't a guarantee. Biotech insiders can be just as wrong about trial data as anyone else.

4. Read the footnotes A "P" can also be a purchase in an underwritten offering at the offering price. That reads very differently from someone hitting "buy" on the open market.

5. Size it against their holdings A $1M sale from someone holding $2B of stock is nothing. A $1M buy from a director whose entire stake was $3M is something.

Live sell-side example: Sea Limited (SE)

Five executives, including CEO Forrest Li and COO Ye Gang, sold about $25.06M between 25 and 28 Aug 2026, all under 10b5-1 plans. The stock then fell 31.3% ($108.68 on 14 Sep → $74.63 on 23 Oct). It looks damning in hindsight, but by this filter it's low signal: planned, small relative to their stakes, and nobody has changed course since.

Source: SEC EDGAR Form 4s. Not advice.

What filters do you use? Anyone actually backtested cluster buys vs. single-insider buys?

Brazilian stock market probably overreacted to election results
This month in international markets saw significant volatility in Brazilian equities. EWZ, which tracks the MSCI Brazil GRTR USD index, surged +12.5% at the beginning of the month, as it priced in the probability of a Flavio Bolsonaro win after a strong showing in round one of the Brazilian elections. However, when the dust had settled, Lula unexpectedly came from behind, and the EWZ gave back all its gains and then some, with a -18.4% drop on Monday.

I wanted to figure out the investors viewed Bolsonaro as so much more market friendly. Curiously, I found that the Brazilian stock market did extremely well during Lula's two prior terms and the third current term and was slightly negative during the presidency of Jair Bolsonaro, the father of losing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro. In Brazil, the presidential terms are four years long and align neatly with the calendar year. This makes it really easy to track returns using the MSCI Brazil, which would be the gold standard anyway. All returns are gross returns using USD currency:

I certainly would not have expected the less market friendly candidate to outperform his counterpart (presumably with similar policies as his son) by such a drastic margin, even after eating that monster -18.4% single day drop this week. However, to be fair, Lula 1 was an incredible time for emerging markets, one which likely could not be reproduced again. And Bolsonaro's presidency coincided with the pandemic, which could have hampered returns.

To control for this, I compared the MSCI Brazil against several other benchmarks to which the country belongs. ACWI includes all countries, ACWI ex-USA is the international market excluding the USA, and emerging markets are the MSCI emerging markets. Additionally, while Brazil does not belong to the MSCI USA, MSCI World (a misnomer which means developed markets including USA), and MSCI World ex-USA (developed markets excluding USA), these are included for comparison. Brazil has trounced all of these benchmarks under Lula's presidency and badly lagged all of them under Jair Bolsonaro.

SpaceX’s 13 GW target implies ~$125B of capex a quarter. How is that funded?

Jensen Huang recently said that a complete 1 GW AI factory costs about $50B. Meanwhile, Elon said on the earning call that he expects SpaceX to reach around 13 GW of compute by the end of 2027, compared with roughly 2.5–3 GW expected by the end of this year. If Jensen’s estimate applies, that additional capacity represents a buildout costing around $500B.

SpaceX reported about $90B in cash and marketable securities at the end of September, and the FT and Reuters reported talks on a further $40B debt package for Nvidia chips. For scale, Q4 capex guidance is $35–40B, up from $19.6B in Q3. A $500B buildout in 2027 implies roughly $125B a quarter, about three times that guidance.

I appreciate that the $500B is only a rough estimate, what I’m struggling to understand is how the business anticipates to raise that money. The CFO says new compute deployments pay back in under a year “at current pricing”, but adding roughly 10 GW in a year means bringing on almost a gigawatt every month. January’s facility can generate cash along the way, but February’s expansion needs funding long before January pays back. How much can those receipts realistically cover, and how much must come from additional borrowing, investors or customers paying upfront?

Has anyone seen a breakdown that connects the capacity targets to the funding required or have any logical theory to make this add up? It seems like an obvious disconnect which makes me think that i'm missing something

text:
Novo Nordisk (NVO) and Madrigal (MDGL) both have something at stake in a new low-dose semaglutide combo
A 16-week phase 2 trial in 62 adults with obesity, treatment-naive type 2 diabetes and MASH found that adding an oral drug called linafexor to weekly semaglutide 0.5 mg more than doubled weight loss versus semaglutide alone. The sponsor is Cascade Pharmaceuticals, which is private.

Source:
https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.18.26365821

What I think this implies:

For Novo Nordisk (NVO) this is a potential way to stretch their GLP-1 further in the type 2 diabetes patients who usually lose less weight on it. Holding the dose at a fraction of the standard obesity amount while still getting better results could mean more patients covered with fewer milligrams, or a better answer for the harder metabolic cases.

For Madrigal Pharmaceuticals (MDGL) it is a competitive risk. Their approved drug Rezdiffra is a standalone MASH therapy used in exactly this obesity-plus-diabetes population, and the trial moved weight, visceral fat and liver enzymes together. If combinations like this become standard, a pure single-mechanism drug loses share.

The practical test for both names is Cascade's separate phase 2 of linafexor alone in MASH plus any announcement of a bigger or longer combination study. Both should happen if the program keeps going, but neither has a public date and the whole thing sits in the 6-24 month window.

It stops being relevant if a larger trial shows the weight-loss difference disappears once semaglutide is raised to normal obesity doses, or if the itching and lipid problems that have limited FXR drugs appear at the exposures already being used in their phase 3 program.

text:
Another Critical Tesla Post - New Info From this Quarter's Earnings Though - Slides Implicated Only ~40 Robotaxis Active

At this point Musk has got to be the biggest pie-in-the-sky salesman the world has ever seen; and, amazingly, people keep buying that pie. Based on its actual 12month earnings Tesla will now have a P/E of 425.

Same general story from this quarter's earnings - fundamentals that make the stock look like a $30 stock but more hype and promises to prop up the price.

Automotive business is essentially flatlined with YoY automotive revenue decreasing -3%. And energy sales - the catalyst many people point to as being able to drive it further - is down 16% to $2.8 billion from $3.4 billion last year.

Additionally, despite touting FSD "take rate" increasing, it appears to have added only $78 million in revenue this quarter, relative to it's total quarter revenue of $28 billion - that is, actual FSD revenue is still minimal.

And, robotaxis - the ever shifting pie in the sky Musk has been touting as something along the lines of an infinite moneyhack - appears to only have about 40 robotaxis operating this entire quarter. More specifically, Tesla's "Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles Chart" on its investor presentation slides implicates about 1.5 million unsupervised robotaxi miles were driven this quarter, for the months of June, July, and August.

The thing is the slides also indicate that robotaxi operating hours in Austin are from 6am to midnight. If you extrapolate that; that's theoretically 18 hours of operating time per robotaxi, one can estimate a low side of miles per hour would be 25 given it's the city; gives 18 hours x 25 mph = 450 miles driven per day per robotaxi x 90 days in the three month period = 40,500 miles per robotaxi driven in the 3 month period. 1,500,000 miles total in the 3 month period / 40,500 miles per robotaxi in that period = the equivalent of 37 robotaxis driving during the entire 3 month period.

Notably, this is a year and a half after Musk claimed robotaxis would be in "half the u.s. population by the end of 2025"

Compare this to Waymo which actually has 4,000 robotaxis on the road and is scaling up. And more and more competitors are coming online or scaling up everyday - including competitors that are using Nvidia tech and hardware - Alpamayo - specifically oriented towards outfitting cars and making them self-driving.

Now, while people are sure to yell "but Tesla can make it's robotaxis at half-the cost of others" consider that Waymo's are getting cheaper and cheaper; and even if Waymos stopped getting cheaper, even where Waymo's currently at just that competition means robotaxi margins won't be that good - which makes sense because, in general, that type of product would be a commodity anyway - that is, everybody wants and will push for cheaper and cheaper cost of transportation as it gets more and more commoditized.

Real world: Tesla now has actual earnings for the past 12 months of $0.91 per share and it's robotaxi business it's turning out is not scaling as fast as others, and there may be no actual moat for that business. I guess there's always optimus (which other robots are ahead of anyway), or a SpaceX buyout at a premium to save the shareprice.

Did anyone actually look at Anthropic's numbers before deciding they were bearish for the AI trade?
The headline was an $80.7bn net loss in six months, which obviously looks terrible but $72bn of that came from a non-cash accounting adjustment related to convertible notes. Ironically, the charge increased because Anthropic's valuation went up and not because the business was deteriorating.

Now look at the underlying business - revenue reached $16.3bn in H1, up from just $1.1bn a year earlier, while the operating loss narrowed to less than $1bn. Operating margins improved from roughly -250% to -5%, even as compute spending quadrupled to nearly $9bn.

Q3 revenue reportedly reached $16.8bn, putting the company on a roughly $67bn annualized run rate.

Thiis says quite a lot about current market sentiment as investors are so focused on finding reasons to sell the AI trade that they are overlooking what is happening underneath.

Anthropic is approaching operating break-even, revenue growth is accelerating, and the company is already generating more revenue than its reported compute costs.

That doesn't mean the enormous infrastructure commitments carry no risk, but the underlying economics are improving much faster than the headline loss suggests.

Bullish

text:
Pinterest (PINS): Fairly Valued at ~$20/share
Company Analysis
I work in marketing, and for most advertisers, Google, Meta and TikTok are where the marketing dollars flow. Beyond that lies the scrapheap of experimental channels: the Reddits, the Snaps and whatever else got a test budget this quarter. At the very bottom of the pile sits Pinterest.

It's been around for over 15 years, and surprisingly enough it makes over $4.5B in revenue with a user base that's slowly but surely growing. Unlike Google and Meta, which have been spending heavily on AI infrastructure, Reddit, which is licensing its content to AI companies, and Snap, which always seems to be in the news for a misguided hardware launches (2K AR glasses anyone) , Pinterest has stayed relatively staid.

I valued it at ~$20/share; and is currently at ~$21.95 today.

Revenue: $4.6B trailing, growing ~16-18% a year; I assume it slows to ~5% and roughly doubles over 10 years.

EBIT margin: ~16% after capitalizing R&D (7.6% reported); I assume it grows to ~20% over 10 years. Meta is at 41%, Reddit 20%.

Net income: $417M in 2025 and ~$250M over the last 12 months, though it dipped to a loss in the first half of 2026 on restructuring and higher stock comp.

Users: 619M monthly users, but US/Canada users generate ~$31 a year each vs. $0.83 for Rest of World.

At ~$20, Pinterest looks fairly priced. If Pinterest can figure out how to make real money from users outside the US and squeeze more profit out of each ad dollar, there's upside here. But if people start asking AI platforms to make purchasing decisions instead of scrolling Pinterest, there isn't.

Let me know if anyone else follows this company or has a different POV from mine.

text:
Tesla and SpaceX already behave like one AI company. Do they need to become one?

SpaceX reports today and Tesla follows on Wednesday. The timing makes the merger speculation difficult to ignore.

The strategic logic is fairly clear. SpaceX brings Starlink, AI computing infrastructure and xAI. Tesla brings the physical platform: cars, robotaxis, energy storage and Optimus.

The Roadster demonstration made that overlap visible. Tesla unveiled a car using SpaceX-developed cold-gas thrusters at a SpaceX facility. It was a dramatic stunt, but also a practical example of technology moving between the two companies.

Put the pieces together and the outline of a vertically integrated AI business starts to appear. SpaceX provides connectivity and compute. Tesla puts that intelligence into machines operating in the real world.

The case against a merger is just as important. Tesla and SpaceX can cooperate through commercial agreements without forcing shareholders to accept a complicated valuation, governance structure and combination of very different risks. SpaceX may also have less to gain from a merger than Tesla.

These earnings should offer more evidence about how dependent the companies are becoming on the same AI strategy.

Does the shared technology justify one corporate structure, or can Tesla and SpaceX capture the same advantages while remaining separate?
label: analysis

The attention economy is a relic of the 2010s and $META is a $1 trillion boomer casino with a GPU addiction

Zuck is about to spend the GDP of a developing nation trying to solve a problem his company is financially incentivized to never solve.

The entire premise of AI is that you can accomplish shit faster. Research something in 10 seconds. Find what you need. Automate tedious tasks. Close the app and go touch grass.

Meta's entire business model is making sure you do absolutely none of those things.

Exhibit A: Instagram. Want to listen to a video with your screen off? Nice try buddy. Get those eyeballs back on the screen, daddy Zuck has ad impressions to serve.

Exhibit B: Facebook Marketplace. This company employs some of the smartest engineers on earth and somehow searching for a $200 table within 15 miles returns a jet ski in Delaware, three Temu dropshippers and a 2006 Nissan Altima with no title. You think this is an accident? I refuse to believe the company building frontier AI cannot implement a few simple filters.

Exhibit C: Facebook itself. An industrial-scale retirement home dopamine dispenser. Your uncle is on hour four of watching AI-generated murder documentaries narrated by a British robot while arguing with a fake veteran about immigration. The algorithm has determined his remaining cognitive capacity is worth approximately $0.17 CPM.

And now Zuck is proposing to “save” people time with his new shopping bot and little AI tool. Sure, users will then have more time to watch reels subtly embedded with more targeted ads. But do people really think Meta is incentivized to help you order a fucking watermelon from Instacart more efficiently?

Here is the actual investment thesis:

AI theoretically eliminates the middleman between wanting something and getting it.

Unfortunately Meta IS the fucking middleman.

If AI makes shopping, searching, and consuming information dramatically faster, plus unbundles how creators find consumers, what happens to a business that makes money when those activities take longer?

You have a trillion-dollar company spending astronomical amounts on compute to build technology that, if it actually works in the consumer's interest, undermines the engagement economics of its own products.

It's like Marlboro spending $100 billion developing a cure for nicotine addiction and then trying to monetize the cure with cigarette ads.

TLDR: Meta is trying to invent the future while its entire business model is trapping divorced dads in a 2014 BuzzFeed slideshow. AI compresses time, Meta sells time. Muse is going to end up having a quicker death than the Metaverse.

Lockheed locks in a third solid rocket motor source for its high volume GMLRS and PrSM lines

Lockheed Martin and Avio announced on 13 October 2026 at the AUSA Annual Meeting a strategic cooperation agreement. Under it Lockheed gains access to a share of the merchant solid rocket motor capacity that Avio's US subsidiary Avio USA is building at a new plant in Hurt Virginia. After qualification the initial work covers motors for the Extended Range GMLRS rocket and the Precision Strike Missile. Avio has launched an investment of more than $500 million in US motor capacity. The Hurt plant broke ground at the end of September 2026 with construction expected to finish in late 2028 and production to start in early 2029. This is the definitive step after a non binding term sheet the two companies signed in November 2025.

Source:
https://breakingdefense.com/2026/10/avio-lockheed-sign-agreement-for-solid-rocket-motor-production/

What I think this implies:

For Lockheed Martin (LMT) this gives contracted access to a third motor source on two of its highest volume munitions programmes. Solid rocket motors are the input both Lockheed and the current suppliers call the limiting layer of the US tactical missile supply chain. A qualified third source would add schedule insurance and more room to negotiate on propulsion once the plant is up.

Northrop Grumman (NOC) took over full contract production of GMLRS rocket motors for Lockheed in 2023 and has been expanding its tactical motor capacity. L3Harris Technologies (LHX) through its Aerojet Rocketdyne subsidiary supplies GMLRS motors to Lockheed under a January 2024 contract. A new merchant supplier competes for motor demand that has had few alternatives so any share that moves to the new plant comes out of their books.

Avio S.p.A. (AVIO) is the parent of the US subsidiary building the Hurt plant behind the stated investment of more than $500 million. Lockheed is now a contracted customer for a share of that capacity once the motors qualify.

The earliest thing to watch is a first firm production order or definitized contract from Lockheed to Avio USA for Extended Range GMLRS or Precision Strike Missile motors disclosed by either company or in Avio's periodic results ahead of the plant's expected completion in late 2028. text:
AWS gives Lambda concurrent-request HTTP with multi-region replication

AWS announced Lambda Web Functions on 12 October 2026. It runs a standard HTTP server without rewriting it as an event handler. Each execution environment serves up to 128 concurrent requests, where existing Event Functions serve one at a time. CPU time is metered actively so time spent waiting on I/O costs little, while memory is billed for the life of the environment. Code is replicated to regions chosen at deploy time with best-effort latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and CloudFront origin access control is supported. It is available today on Node.js 24 on Arm64 in five regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio), US West (Oregon), Tokyo and Ireland.

Source:
https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/announcing-aws-lambda-web-functions-for-fast-consistent-web-app-performance-anywhere/

Here's what I think this implies:

Amazon operates Lambda and is the vendor shipping Web Functions, the form factor that extends its serverless product into standard HTTP application hosting. Cloudflare's Workers runtime is the established product for running HTTP applications concurrently across globally distributed locations, the specific execution model AWS has now built into Lambda, so exposure runs against Cloudflare if AWS converts Lambda's installed base rather than losing it. Fastly markets Compute as its edge serverless runtime for HTTP workloads and competes for the same developer deployments, so exposure runs against it if those deployments consolidate onto Lambda.

The catalyst is AWS extending Web Functions beyond the five launch regions and the single Node.js 24 Arm64 runtime, and the next quarterly results and developer-platform announcements from Cloudflare and Fastly, where a hyperscaler offering concurrent-request HTTP serverless with regional replication would have to be addressed.

If AWS leaves Web Functions on one runtime in five regions with best-effort routing, it cannot host the polyglot, globally distributed workloads that sit on edge runtimes today, and the competitive reading fails. If the active-CPU billing turns out to be offset by memory billed for the life of a long-lived environment, the cost argument for migrating web applications onto it disappears.

text:
Why it’s bad to trade frequently (even if we ignore transaction fees and the difference between short vs long term capital gains)
Advice
For a long time, I assumed the following two scenarios are mathematically equivalent (ignoring transaction fees and assuming only long term capital gains applies):
- buying a position, holding it for a long time, then selling it for a gain
- buying a position, selling mid way through then buying it back at the same share price as the sale, then holding it the rest of the way then sell

The reason my intuition said these scenarios should have the identical outcome is because you’ll eventually need to pay taxes on all of the gains anyway, what’s the difference of recognizing a portion of the gains early?

A few days ago, I wanted to check my intuition, so I came up with a thought experiment. For ease of explanation, let’s say capital gains tax is a flat 20%.
- scenario 1: buy $100 of a stock, it doubles, I hold, then it doubles again, I sell for a total of $400. I pay $60 in tax (20% x $300), so I end up with $340.
- scenario 2: buy $100 of a stock, it doubles, I sell for a total of $200, pay $20 in tax, then use the remaining $180 to buy it back at the same share price as the sale. It then doubles again, I sell for a total of $360, pay $36 in tax, and end up with $324.

If you repeat this experiment with other tax rates, the two scenarios are identical only when the tax rate is 0% or 100%, and for any other tax rate between these two extremes, scenario 1 comes out ahead.

This result may be intuitive to some, but it wasn’t to me. This really made me appreciate just how much of an uphill battle it would be if you wanted to beat the market by trading.

text:
The AI capex boom is increasingly a bet on AGI, not current economics

I think analysts are missing something big by considering AI frontier labs as though they were normal companies making big investments and expecting realistic business outcomes. I want to posit that the AI bubble differs from earlier bubbles because the spending is being justified by quasi-religious beliefs about what AI might eventually become. After reading Adam Becker's More Everything Forever, I’ve started to see the frontier AI race as a billionaire-funded cargo cult: the belief that if enough GPUs, power, data centers, researchers, and capital are accumulated, something qualitatively new will emerge, an AGI or superintelligence that equates to a machine god.

It's basically a science-fiction investment thesis. It sounds crazy, but there's a literal network of rationalist, effective-altruist, and existential-risk thinkers who've spent years treating AGI as a civilization-altering event long before ChatGPT arrived, and those ideas have shaped many of the companies, investors, and researchers now driving the industry. You can verify this. If AGI is truly only a few years away, almost any level of spending can seem rational: frontier labs do not need sustainable business models today because losing billions is preferable to slowing down and letting a competitor reach the prize first.

AI is not fake or useless. LLMs can write code, summarize documents, automate office work, and support research, even if the economics are shaky on some of it. The problem is the belief that models will turn into superintelligent 'beings' if we just pour enough resources into them. I suspect some big players know this: NVIDIA is happy to profit by selling the infrastructure even if Jensen knows its bullshit, Microsoft through Mustafa Suleyman has basically called BS on a lot of this, Google falls somewhere in the middle, and Meta is trying to turn it into a useful consumer product (which I also don't think will work, but that's another issue). In the end, most customers will care less about AGI than whether AI saves enough money to justify the bill.

The bubble bursting will still hurt these companies, but in the end I think may come out okay in the end, but there may be pain along the way. OpenAI and Anthropic are a lot shakier, and I'm curious to see how long they can drag this out: it could be a while. Look how long Elon has been pumping pipe dreams that never happen.

Disclosures: I own MSFT and NVDA.

(21 Oct - Yahoo Finance) Anthropic is set to publicly file its S-1 investor prospectus as soon as Friday, according to three people familiar with the artificial intelligence firm's plans. The move would mark a crucial next step for what could be the biggest IPO in history.

The much-anticipated public debut, expected to surpass SpaceX's (SPCX) June IPO, is widely viewed as a crucial test of investor appetite for the artificial intelligence boom, as investors have become more concerned about the industry's massive spending.

Anthropic confidentially submitted a draft IPO registration statement to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in June. Under SEC rules, companies using the confidential process must make their registration materials available 15 calendar days before the start of their formal investor roadshow.

Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment on the timing of its S-1.

A public filing would clear a key procedural hurdle toward a potential November listing, though the timing of the offering remains subject to market conditions and other factors. Crucially, it would also give regular investors their first look at the financial details and risks around one of the AI industry's fastest-growing companies.

Anthropic is spending billions on AI infrastructure to train and run its suite of Claude models. That includes working with Google (GOOG, GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN), as well as renting out graphics processor unit (GPU) capacity from SpaceX's Colossus 1 data center.

The company pulled in $16.3 billion in revenue over the first six months of 2026 and reported a net loss of over $80 billion, according to a Tuesday Wall Street Journal report. Wall Street is anticipating that the company could raise as much as $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation, Reuters previously reported.

Last week, Anthropic told investors at its San Francisco office that its revenue climbed to $16.8 billion in the third quarter, up from $11.5 billion in the second quarter, according to the Financial Times, noting that the company is also profitable on an adjusted basis.

The colossal offering comes as this year's banner IPO market is becoming more challenging. Earlier this week, shares of South Korean data center provider Elice plummeted a staggering 32% during its first trading day after raising $151 million. Nvidia-backed Firmus Grid abruptly shelved plans for a public listing earlier this month after investors balked at its proposed valuation, while several other companies have postponed plans to go public, citing market conditions.

OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while ​Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI's funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said.

Investors familiar with the company say OpenAI also needs capital ​to fund its substantial infrastructure commitments and bolster its balance sheet if a deterioration in the IPO markets further delays its planned 2027 listing.

text:
Passenger vehicle shipments from manufacturers in China fell 8.9% year over year in September while exports within them rose 73.7%
Domestic passenger vehicle retail dropped 28% from a year earlier in September, a much steeper decline than total shipments posted. The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) published the September data on October 12. Wholesale covers what manufacturers shipped in the month, domestic deliveries and exports, not end purchases, and it fell 8.9% year over year while manufacturer-reported passenger vehicle exports grew 73.7%. With those year-over-year numbers side by side, I read them as exports offsetting some of the domestic decline, and exports' share of wholesale went from 19% a year earlier to 36%.

Against the prior month, the export share dropped two months running from 41% in July, while September wholesale and exports both rose, which does not sit as neatly with that reading. The CPCA named ten automakers as NEV exporters, meaning battery electric, plug-in hybrid and range-extended vehicles, and those exports also rose from August. BYD's figure fell while Chery and Leapmotor gained, and these are shipments abroad only, not counting combustion-engine exports.

The CPCA pointed to this year's Mid-Autumn Festival falling earlier than usual, in late September, with clearly weaker domestic sales that week. It cited a high base from September 2025, when subsidies for car buyers in some provinces were about to expire and purchases concentrated before they lapsed. The report listed other causes, and how much of the retail drop those two explain is not clear from one month.

On October 12 the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration announced a reduction in the export VAT rebate rate for battery electric and plug-in hybrid passenger vehicles. The rate drops from 13% to 9%. It applies to exports from April 1, 2027, going by the export date. The announcement does not settle how large the effect will be.

The CPCA report carries two export counts. For August, manufacturer-reported passenger vehicle exports including kits for overseas assembly rose 77.8% from a year earlier, while customs data for all vehicle types grew 37%. No September customs figure appears. What would you watch in the report covering October data, out next month, to gauge what exports are doing for automakers' total shipments with domestic volume down?

Of the automakers on the CPCA's September NEV export list, two are in CNQQ and the other eight are not. The latest issuer holdings file puts BYD at about 1.75% of net assets, held as the Shenzhen-listed A share, and XPeng at roughly 0.41%. CQQQ's index is a FTSE benchmark of Chinese companies the provider classifies under technology.

text:
Robotis Teams Up with Nvidia to Kick Off Mass Production of 10,000 Humanoids a Year

Robotis has partnered with Nvidia to unveil real-world task capabilities for its humanoid "AI Sapiens" and has begun building a production system targeting 10,000 units annually. At the Humanoid Summit Seoul 2026 held at COEX on the 22nd, Robotis announced its open humanoid platform strategy and showcased how it used Nvidia's Cosmos Transfer to resolve a shadow misidentification problem with synthetic data. Nvidia unveiled its general-purpose robot intelligence model GR00T 1.7 and the development roadmap for next-generation GR00T 2, presenting a "data pyramid" strategy.

Kim Byung-soo, founder and CEO of Robotis, laid out a vision in his keynote to establish humanoids as a platform where diverse applications perform multiple functions, much like smartphones did in the past. He explained that while automating 100 different tasks once required 100 different types of robots, advances in AI now allow a single robot to handle multiple tasks.

Robotis plans to significantly expand AI Sapiens production starting next year, aiming to scale humanoid manufacturing to an annual rate of 10,000 units. The company's mass production strategy rests on two pillars: high-volume hardware manufacturing and a software ecosystem that enables a single robot to rapidly learn multiple tasks.

On the hardware side, Robotis plans to sequentially release a lineup of roughly 70 actuator models beginning early next year. At the event, AI Sapiens took the stage to demonstrate boxing and squat motions, showcasing the stability of its joint actuation.

Kim compared AI Sapiens to Unitree's G1, noting that "the height is similar at around 136 cm, and the weight is the same," but emphasized that "the higher actuator efficiency gives it the advantage of more than double the battery operating time."

As humanoid production scales up, learning efficiency is expected to become even more critical. Collecting real-world task data for each individual robot requires equipment, operators, time, and space. Robotis is also pursuing a parallel approach: extracting motion from human video or text, training simultaneously across thousands of virtual environments, and then applying the results to physical robots.

Raytheon showed a rocket-powered version of its Coyote counter-drone interceptor

Raytheon unveiled the Coyote Block 2C+RM. Current Block 2 versions use a rocket only to get off the rail, then fly on a small turbojet. This one is rocket-powered the whole way. Raytheon says that buys a faster launch, higher speed, and more range, plus better performance when it has to close on a target. It also has a new seeker and a new warhead. The variant has been in development for about fifteen months. The motor, supplied by an unnamed subcontractor, has been static-fired, and there have been three successful live test launches.

The nearest test is the Army's low-cost interceptor shoot-off, reported as planned for November 2026. Raytheon has more tests scheduled into the first half of 2027. The deciding step is an Army order or programme decision that names the Block 2C+RM specifically.

If the next counter-drone awards go to other designs instead of a Coyote variant, or if the real unit price of this version ends up close to a conventional surface-to-air missile, the argument that it solves the magazine-depth problem at lower cost does not hold.

text:
Airbus and Kratos flew a European version of the XQ-58A, putting it in the mix for Germany's first jet combat drone

Airbus and Kratos announced the first flight of the U740 Valkyrie, a Europeanised version of Kratos' American XQ-58A uncrewed combat aircraft. It took off with rocket assistance, flew at several altitudes up to Mach 0.8, and Airbus says all test objectives were met. The airframe already exists and flies. The part that would make it European, Airbus' own MARS mission system, has not flown on it yet. That is the next phase.

Germany has been slow to field armed drones and is looking at three options: this adapted American airframe, Boeing's MQ-28 Ghost Bat with Rheinmetall as the integrator, and Helsing's homegrown CA-1 Europa. This flight moves the Valkyrie path forward because the plane is already flying. The remaining work is the European software layer.

Airbus is adapting the airframe and owns the MARS system, so a German buy would depend on that work. Kratos designed and builds the XQ-58A the U740 is based on, and would supply the aircraft itself. Rheinmetall is the system integrator on the rival Ghost Bat offer, so that work goes away if Germany picks the Valkyrie. Hensoldt supplies sensors and mission-system parts to both rival bids and is not on this one. Helsing is private.

The companies say they are on track for a combat-ready aircraft by 2029. No German contract has been announced. The government was reported in August to be aiming for a selection in 2027. The first clear step is a flight that carries the MARS system. The deciding one is which offer Germany picks.

If Germany takes the Ghost Bat or the CA-1 instead, or pushes the decision past 2027, this path produces no production. The same happens if the MARS flights slip or show the European software cannot command the airframe without American-controlled software.

Elon Musk called it “the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America.”

The plan is to combine satellites with a ground-based mobile network. The low-band airwaves would complement Starlink’s 2 GHz spectrum, helping improve indoor coverage and extend service into areas with weak or nonexistent cellular reception. That would put Starlink in more direct competition with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.

Separately, the FCC approved a new constellation of 15,000 SpaceX satellites this week for direct-to-device mobile services, another step toward expanding Starlink’s ability to connect directly to phones.

The spectrum acquisition still requires FCC approval and other customary closing conditions. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Nvidia, Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sink on OpenAI revenue report

Shares of Nvidia, Oracle, CoreWeave and other artificial intelligence names sank lower on Thursday after the market learned more details about OpenAI’s revenue.

OpenAI told investors that it hit roughly $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, CNBC confirmed, lower than the the $68 billion figure that was widely reported late last month. A person familiar with the matter said the $68 billion figure included gross revenue from OpenAI’s partners, which helps investors make a more direct comparison with its chief rival, Anthropic.

The Financial Times was first to report the $50 billion figure.

OpenAI shared an update about its finances in an investor presentation, said the person, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the numbers. In addition to the $50 billion in annualized revenue, OpenAI touted 77% total run rate growth during its third quarter, as well as 107% run rate growth for its enterprise business during the same period, the person said.

The company is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation to investors as it gears up for what is widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June, and executives have signaled that the company is eyeing a 2027 debut.

Samsung forecasts record third-quarter profit of $80 billion for the first time in history - Operating profit jumped 782%

Samsung Electronics on Thursday reported third-quarter preliminary operating profit of 107.40 trillion won ($80.2 billion), surging past 100 trillion won for the first time in the company’s history as booming demand for artificial intelligence continues to fuel its chips business.

Quarterly operating profit jumped 782% from a year earlier. Revenue came in at about 195 trillion won, up nearly 127% from the same period last year.

Samsung, the world’s largest memory chipmaker, has benefited from surging demand for memory used in AI infrastructure. In the second quarter, the company posted record revenue of 171.5 trillion won and record operating profit of 89.5 trillion won, driven by its memory business.
The company has also stepped up investments and partnerships tied to AI. In September, Samsung announced a strategic partnership with French artificial intelligence startup Mistral AI, with plans to deploy the startup’s AI models across its semiconductor operations.

FCC approves $SPCX to deploy 15,000 Starlink satellites for D2C service

The FCC has approved SpaceX to deploy up to 15,000 next-generation Starlink satellites, enabling direct-to-cell service with speeds of up to 150 Mbps and full 5G capabilities.

The low-Earth orbit constellation (326-335 km altitude) will support supplemental coverage in the US, direct-to-cell globally, and higher data speeds using spectrum acquired from EchoStar.

The decision includes a waiver enabling SpaceX to offer satellite-based mobile service independently of terrestrial carriers, advancing Starlink’s expansion into phone connectivity. ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
